blocks.content: Filtering logic has a way of quietly growing out of control. What starts as one clean if statement checking whether a product is in stock slowly picks up a price check, then a category check, then a seasonal discount check, until nobody wants to touch that method again. The Specification pattern exists to stop that growth before it starts.
1. Introduction & Why It Matters

The Specification pattern encapsulates a single business rule or query condition as its own object, with one method, isSatisfiedBy, that answers a yes or no question about a candidate. Instead of one method checking five things at once, you get five small specification objects, each responsible for exactly one rule.

What makes the pattern powerful is composition: specifications combine with AND, OR and NOT to build up arbitrarily complex logic from small, already tested pieces. Add a new rule to the system and you write one new class, you never have to reopen and retest the rules that already exist.
2. Real-Life Analogy
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784889855086-437772329.png
blocks.alt: A bouncer checking age, a valid ID and the guest list as three independent rules that all must pass before entry

blocks.content: Picture a nightclub bouncer working the door. They are not running one giant mental checklist all mashed together, they are running three completely separate, independent checks: is this person 21 or older, do they have a valid ID, and are they on the guest list for tonight. Each check stands alone, the bouncer could swap out the guest list rule for a different one tomorrow night without changing how the age check or the ID check works at all. Only when every single check passes does the person get waved inside, that is an AND composition of independent specifications, exactly what the pattern models in code.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784889857129-510847801.png
blocks.alt: A bank loan officer checking credit score, income and existing debt as separate independent criteria before approving a loan

blocks.content: A bank loan approval works the same way. A loan officer checks a credit score threshold, checks that income comfortably covers the repayment, and checks that existing debt is not too high, three independent criteria, each one owned by a different rule. Swap the credit score threshold for a stricter one during a downturn, and the income check and the debt check do not need to change at all, because each criterion never knew anything about the others in the first place.
3. Problem It Solves & Definition

Real applications accumulate business rules constantly: a product must be in stock, under a price limit, in the right category, and not already discontinued, all at once, and the exact combination of rules often changes from one screen or report to the next. Writing every combination as its own if statement or its own query method does not scale, you end up with either one giant unreadable condition or dozens of near duplicate methods that each hardcode a slightly different mix of the same underlying rules.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.content: The Specification pattern is a design pattern that encapsulates a single business rule or query criterion inside its own object with one method, isSatisfiedBy, and allows multiple specifications to be combined with AND, OR and NOT into more complex rules. In simple terms: turn every yes or no rule into its own small, combinable object instead of a branch inside a bigger method.
4. Key Terminology

["Specification: an object that encapsulates a single business rule or query condition behind one method, isSatisfiedBy.","isSatisfiedBy(candidate): the one method every specification implements, returning true when the candidate matches the rule.","Candidate: the object being tested against a specification, for example a single Product instance.","Composite specification: a specification built by combining other specifications together, such as AndSpecification, OrSpecification or NotSpecification.","AND composition: a combined specification that is satisfied only when every wrapped specification is satisfied.","OR composition: a combined specification that is satisfied when at least one wrapped specification is satisfied."]
items: Specification: an object that encapsulates a single business rule or query condition behind one method, isSatisfiedBy.
isSatisfiedBy(candidate): the one method every specification implements, returning true when the candidate matches the rule.
Candidate: the object being tested against a specification, for example a single Product instance.
Composite specification: a specification built by combining other specifications together, such as AndSpecification, OrSpecification or NotSpecification.
AND composition: a combined specification that is satisfied only when every wrapped specification is satisfied.
OR composition: a combined specification that is satisfied when at least one wrapped specification is satisfied.

blocks.content: 5. Visual Diagram
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784889858840-49555301.png
blocks.alt: The Specification interface with InStockSpecification and PriceBelowSpecification as concrete rules, combined by an AndSpecification

blocks.content: Every concrete specification implements the same interface, one method, isSatisfiedBy. AndSpecification is a specification too, except instead of checking the candidate itself, it holds two other specifications and simply asks both of them, returning true only when both agree.
6. Syntax & Code Example

A specification needs just one method, isSatisfiedBy, on a shared interface. Every concrete rule implements that interface, and a combinator like AndSpecification implements it too, except instead of checking the candidate directly, it delegates to two other specifications and combines their answers:

["Specification interface: declares a single method, isSatisfiedBy, that takes a candidate and returns true or false.","Concrete specification: a small class implementing that interface, each one responsible for exactly one independent rule.","AndSpecification: a specification that stores two other specifications and returns true only when both of their isSatisfiedBy calls return true for the same candidate."]
items: Specification interface: declares a single method, isSatisfiedBy, that takes a candidate and returns true or false.
Concrete specification: a small class implementing that interface, each one responsible for exactly one independent rule.
AndSpecification: a specification that stores two other specifications and returns true only when both of their isSatisfiedBy calls return true for the same candidate.

["Specification interface: declares one method, isSatisfiedBy, that every concrete specification must implement.","InStockSpecification: checks a single, independent rule, whether the product is currently in stock.","PriceBelowSpecification: checks a second independent rule, whether the price is under a given limit, using its own stored limit field.","AndSpecification: wraps two specifications and is satisfied only when both of them return true for the same candidate.","The loop in main: tests every product against one combined specification instead of writing a single tangled if statement that checks both conditions at once."]
items: Specification interface: declares one method, isSatisfiedBy, that every concrete specification must implement.
InStockSpecification: checks a single, independent rule, whether the product is currently in stock.
PriceBelowSpecification: checks a second independent rule, whether the price is under a given limit, using its own stored limit field.
AndSpecification: wraps two specifications and is satisfied only when both of them return true for the same candidate.
The loop in main: tests every product against one combined specification instead of writing a single tangled if statement that checks both conditions at once.

Laptop and Headphones satisfy both wrapped rules at once and make it into the filtered result. Phone fails the stock check alone, and Tablet fails the price check alone, either single failure is enough to make the whole AndSpecification return false for that candidate.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784889862236-397165149.png

blocks.content: That is the entire benefit of the pattern in one dry run: one combined specification correctly separates the products that satisfy every rule from the ones that fail even a single check, without a single tangled if statement anywhere in sight.
9. Behind the Scenes (Specifications as a Composite Tree)
blocks.text: 9. Behind the Scenes (Specifications as a Composite Tree)

blocks.content: Composing specifications with AND, OR and NOT is not magic, underneath, a combinator is just another specification that happens to hold references to other specifications instead of checking the candidate itself.
9.1 Every Combinator Wraps Other Specifications

AndSpecification stores exactly two specifications, first and second, and its own isSatisfiedBy simply calls isSatisfiedBy on both and combines the answers with a boolean AND. Nest an AndSpecification inside another AndSpecification, or mix in an OrSpecification, and you get a tree of specifications, each node only ever knowing about its own direct children.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784889864008-128651926.png
blocks.alt: AndSpecification wrapping InStockSpecification and PriceBelowSpecification, each running isSatisfiedBy before the results combine

blocks.content: Walking that tree for a single candidate is exactly what the diagram shows: each wrapped specification runs its own isSatisfiedBy independently, and only once both answers are known does the AndSpecification combine them into one final true or false.
9.2 Order, Short-Circuiting and Reusability

Most languages evaluate the boolean AND with short circuiting, so if the first wrapped specification already returns false, the second one never even runs. That is a real reason to put the cheaper or more likely to fail check first when you build a combinator by hand. None of this changes the fact that InStockSpecification and PriceBelowSpecification remain fully independent, either one can be reused inside a completely different combination, or tested entirely on its own, without ever touching AndSpecification at all.
10. Real-World Use Cases & Industry Examples
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784889865737-490798619.png
blocks.alt: Fixed independent rules modeled as specifications across e-commerce, banking, social media and gaming domains

items: E-commerce: a product search filter combines specifications like InStockSpecification, PriceBelowSpecification and CategorySpecification, letting shoppers stack any combination of filters without the backend writing a brand new query for every combination.
Banking: fraud detection rules such as LargeTransactionSpecification and UnusualLocationSpecification combine with OR, so a transaction gets flagged the moment any single suspicious rule matches.
Social Media: a content moderation pipeline combines specifications such as ContainsBannedWordSpecification and ReportedByMultipleUsersSpecification to decide whether a post needs manual review.
Gaming: a matchmaking system combines specifications like SkillRangeSpecification and RegionSpecification to decide which players can be grouped into the same match.

blocks.content: This same idea is not just a hand-rolled interface, it ships directly inside a framework used in production systems every day:
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784889867338-387995868.png
blocks.alt: Spring Data JPA using a Specification interface whose toPredicate method builds a dynamic WHERE clause at query time

blocks.content: Spring Data JPA ships a real Specification interface with one method, toPredicate, playing exactly the same role as isSatisfiedBy here, except it builds a JPA Criteria Predicate instead of returning a plain boolean. A repository that extends JpaSpecificationExecutor can accept any combination of specifications chained together with and, or and negation helpers, letting an application compose dynamic SQL filters from small, independently tested pieces, the same idea as the bouncer checklist from earlier, just aimed at a database query instead of a person at a door.
11. Advantages & Limitations

{"headers":["Advantages","Limitations"],"rows":[["Each rule becomes an isolated, independently testable object instead of a branch buried inside one large method.","Introduces a brand new class for every single rule, which can feel heavy for a one-off check used in exactly one place."],["New rules combine with AND, OR and NOT without ever touching or risking the existing, already tested specifications.","Deeply nested combinations of specifications can become just as hard to read as the tangled conditional they replaced."],["The exact same specification object can be reused across a search filter, a validation check and a reporting query.","Naive implementations recompute an entire specification chain repeatedly instead of caching or short circuiting once a result is already known."]]}
12. Common Mistakes & Best Practices
12.1 Common Mistakes

["Building one giant AndSpecification with ten different rules squeezed into a single isSatisfiedBy method, recreating the exact tangled conditional the pattern was meant to replace.","Giving a specification hidden side effects, like logging or sending a notification inside isSatisfiedBy, when it should only ever answer a yes or no question about the candidate.","Hardcoding a fixed comparison value inside a specification instead of storing it as a field, which makes the same rule impossible to reuse with a different threshold.","Reimplementing AND and OR combination logic by hand at every call site instead of writing one reusable AndSpecification and OrSpecification a single time."]
items: Building one giant AndSpecification with ten different rules squeezed into a single isSatisfiedBy method, recreating the exact tangled conditional the pattern was meant to replace.
Giving a specification hidden side effects, like logging or sending a notification inside isSatisfiedBy, when it should only ever answer a yes or no question about the candidate.
Hardcoding a fixed comparison value inside a specification instead of storing it as a field, which makes the same rule impossible to reuse with a different threshold.
Reimplementing AND and OR combination logic by hand at every call site instead of writing one reusable AndSpecification and OrSpecification a single time.

blocks.content: 12.2 Best Practices

["Keep each concrete specification focused on exactly one rule, and name it after that rule directly, like InStockSpecification.","Implement AndSpecification, OrSpecification and NotSpecification once as generic combinators that work with any specification of the same candidate type.","Unit test every concrete specification in isolation, with at least one candidate that should pass and one that should fail.","Put the cheaper, more likely to fail check first inside a combined AndSpecification, so failing candidates get rejected as early as possible."]
items: Keep each concrete specification focused on exactly one rule, and name it after that rule directly, like InStockSpecification.
Implement AndSpecification, OrSpecification and NotSpecification once as generic combinators that work with any specification of the same candidate type.
Unit test every concrete specification in isolation, with at least one candidate that should pass and one that should fail.
Put the cheaper, more likely to fail check first inside a combined AndSpecification, so failing candidates get rejected as early as possible.

blocks.content: 13. Key Takeaways & Cheat Sheet

["The Specification pattern wraps a single business rule behind one method, isSatisfiedBy, so the rule can be tested, reused and combined on its own.","AndSpecification, OrSpecification and NotSpecification let you build arbitrarily complex filtering logic out of small, already tested pieces.","Adding a brand new rule never requires editing or risking any of the existing specifications, you just write one new class.","The pattern trades a small amount of extra class overhead for rules that are independently testable, reusable and easy to recombine."]
items: The Specification pattern wraps a single business rule behind one method, isSatisfiedBy, so the rule can be tested, reused and combined on its own.
AndSpecification, OrSpecification and NotSpecification let you build arbitrarily complex filtering logic out of small, already tested pieces.
Adding a brand new rule never requires editing or risking any of the existing specifications, you just write one new class.
The pattern trades a small amount of extra class overhead for rules that are independently testable, reusable and easy to recombine.

blocks.title: Interview tip
blocks.content: If asked why not just write one big if statement instead of the Specification pattern, the fastest correct answer is: a giant conditional cannot be tested rule by rule, reused across different parts of the codebase, or extended with a new rule without touching and risking every existing check, a Specification object can do all three.
